=== CONTEXT (do NOT extract rows from this part; use only to identify the section headers in effect) ===
 A.G.

The Deputy Superintendent General of Indian Affairs, Ottawa.

Travelling Expenses of Ottawa Officials should be paid from Civil Government Contingencies

AUDIT OFFICE, OTTAWA, October 11, 1923.

SIR, - I have before me two accounts, amounting to $780.62, for the expenses of Mr. D.F. Robertson, chief surveyor of
your department, when visiting Brantford between January 24th and March 20th last. I understand from your
accounting branch that Mr. Robertson was acting as agent at the Six Nations Reserve during that period. In these
accounts I find several items to which I have to take exception.

No vouchers or receipts are given in support of the following payments:

Jan. 27th, Kerby House, board and lodging $11 50
Feb 9th, Kerby House, board and lodging 61 78

Receipted vouchers showing in detail how these amounts are arrived at should be furnished by Mr. Robertson.

On four occasions during the period covered by Mr. Robertson's accounts he appears to have returned to Ottawa for the
week end, arriving in Ottawa on Saturday morning and leaving again on Sunday night, at a cost of approximately $30
for each trip. I should like to be assured that each of these week end trips was necessarily undertaken on departmental
business.

In connection with these week end trips I notice that Mr. Robertson makes the following charges for meals at Ottawa:

January 28 $3 75
January 29 3 75
February 10 2 75
February 11 3 75
February 25 3 75
February 26 3 75
March 21 1 25
...         $22 75



=== EXTRACT FROM HERE (pages 590-593) ===
<!-- page 590 -->
As Mr Robertson's headquarters are supposed to be at Ottawa, these charges cannot be allowed and should be
refunded.

In the hotel bill at Brantford paid on March 17th, amounting to $26.05, there is a charge of $1.55 for laundry which
cannot be allowed and should be refunded.

Mr. Robertson's expenses have been charged to your vote for Ontario and Quebec; as he is an Ottawa official I have to
ask why these expenses were not paid from Civil Government Contingencies, in accordance to the Order-in-Council of
November 7th, 1912.


I am, sir, your obedient servant,
WM. KEARNS, Asst. A.G.

The Deputy Superintendent General of Indian Affairs, Ottawa.

DEPARTMENT OF INDIAN AFFAIRS, OTTAWA, October 19, 1923.

SIR, - With reference to your letter of the 11th instant, respecting Mr. D.F. Robertson's accounts when visiting
Brantford, I beg to enclose for your information a copy of a memorandum from him which I trust will afford you the
information you require.

With reference to the last paragraph of your letter asking why these expenses were not charged to Civil Government
Contingencies, I have to say that they were so charged in the first place, but were afterwards transferred to the Ontario
and Quebec Vote, as it was found that the appropriation for expenses under Civil Government Contingencies would
not bear the charges unless a supplementary vote was obtained, which it was desired to avoid. Furthermore as Mr.
Robertson was Acting Indian Agent at Brantford pro tem, it was considered that that Agency should properly be
charged with these expenses.


Your obedient servant,
J.D. MCLEAN, Asst. Deputy and Secretary.

The Assistant Auditor General.

AUDIT OFFICE, OTTAWA, October 30, 1923.

SIR, - I am in receipt of your letter of the 19th inst. (No. 112 - 75) in reply to mine of the 11th with regard to the
expenses of Mr. D.F. Robertson when visiting Brantford in January, February and March last.

The explanation given by Mr. Robertson of his various trips to Ottawa may be regarded as satisfactory. With regard to
the living expenses at Ottawa, I would say that while there may be some reason for allowing them in this case still
such charges should be watched very carefully and allowed only in very exceptional circumstances, as the practice is
one that would be very apt to be abused.

The reasons given in your letter for charging these expenses to the Ontario and Quebec vote instead of to Civil
Government Contingencies, viz., (1) That the vote for Civil Government Contingencies would not bear the charge
without a supplementary vote being obtained and (2) that as Mr. Robertson was Acting

<!-- page 591 -->
Indian Agent it was considered that the agency should be charged with his expenses, cannot be considered sufficient:
the Order in Council of November 7th, 1913, directs that the expenses of all Ottawa officials be charged against Civil
Government Contingencies; if it were desired to charge such expenses against any other vote special authority to do so
should have been obtained from Council.

I am, sir, your obedient servant,
WM. KEARNS, Asst. A.G.

The Deputy Superintendent General of Indian Affairs, Ottawa.

Payment of Balance for Church Built in 1911
AUDIT OFFICE, OTTAWA, June 14, 1923.

SIR, - Indian Trust Fund Cheque No. 1977, issued on June 14th, 1922, is for a payment of $448.46 from the Capital
funds of the Shawanaga band of Indians to Mr. Louis Kaufman, being the balance due him for the construction of a
church which he completed in 1911 for the Roman Catholic members of the band.

Payment of the balance appears to have been duly sanctioned by the members of the band, and has been authorized by
the Governor-in-Council. I should however, like to have an explanation of the delay of eleven years in meeting this
indebtedness.

I am, Sir, your obedient servant,
WM. KEARNS, Asst. A.G.

The Deputy Superintendent General of Indian Affairs, Ottawa.

DEPARTMENT OF INDIAN AFFAIRS OTTAWA, June 21, 1923.

DEAR SIR, - In reply to your letter of the 14th instant, asking why eleven years were allowed to lapse before payment
was made to Mr. Louis Kaufman for building a Roman Catholic church at Shawanaga, I beg to say that when the
building of a church was undertaken, payment was to be made by the Indians and to assist them permits were issued to
cut sufficient logs to exchange for lumber for this church.

The plans of the original church were changed and an addition as a residence for the priest was erected. This residence
was necessary as the priest visits the reserve for a few days at stated periods and there was no home convenient for his
accommodation. Mr. Kaufman supplied extra lumber and hardware, also paid for labour, thus increasing the cost of the
building to $852.92, and received payment in logs to the value of $404.46 only, thus leaving an expenditure made by
Mr. Kaufman of $448.46 for which he was not reimbursed.

Mr. Kaufman and the Indians tried to arrange matters but it was impossible for the Indians to make payment unless the
money was raised by illegally cutting logs.

1 - 16 I

<!-- page 592 -->
The Department could not allow this, consequently when the matter was referred to the Department in 1921 for
settlement and it was ascertained that the Indians were all in favour of paying Mr. Kaufman, as evidenced by the
resolution of the Indian Council passed on the 21st November, 1921, it was decided to grant their request.

Order-in-Council was obtained 9th June, 1922, granting authority to pay Mr. Kaufman the balance owing to him and
accordingly cheque No. 1977 for $448.46 was issued in Mr. Kaufman's favour.

Yours truly,
J.D. MCLEAN, Asst. Deputy and Secretary.

WM. KEARNS, Asst. Auditor General.

Re-embursement for Expenses arising out of Cancelled Sale.

AUDIT OFFICE, OTTAWA, October 9, 1923.

SIR, - Ontario and Quebec cheque No. 274 issued on May 29th, 1922, is for the payment of $81.55 to Carroll Haffell
Powell of Kingston, for disbursements by him in connection with the sale to him of Little Horseshoe Island, which sale
was subsequently cancelled.

I should like to have a full explanation of the circumstances leading up to this payment, together with any evidence
you may have that the disbursements claimed by Mr. Powell were actually made by him, particularly with regard to the
item of $50 charged in connection with a harbour for motor boat.

I notice that the account was certified to by the Justice Department on January 24th, 1923, some months after it had
actually been paid. As this is not an account for legal services rendered your department, am I right in inferring that the
intention of this certificate was to show that in the opinion of the Justice Department, Mr. Powell had a legal claim for
$81.55 against your department.

I am, sir, your obedient servant,
WM. KEARNS, Asst. A.G.

The Deputy Superintendent General of Indian Affairs, Ottawa.

DEPARTMENT OF INDIAN AFFAIRS, OTTAWA, October 12, 1923.

SIR, - I beg to acknowledge the receipt of your letter of the 9th instant, with respect to Ontario and Quebec cheque
No. 274, issued on May 29th, 1922, for the sum of $81.55, to one Carroll Haffell Powell, of Kingston, for certain
disbursements made by him in connection with the sale to him of Little Horse Shoe Island, which sale was
subsequently cancelled.

This Department on the 2nd day of August, 1921, sold what is known as Island No. 3 in Lake Ontario to one Carroll
Haffell Powell, and subsequent investigation convinced the Department that the sale was made in error, in that this
island No. 3 was at the time of survey in 1863 considered a part of what is known as Horse Shoe Island, and as such
was included in a patent covering the western portion of the island, which patent issued to one James Eccles, on the
5th day of December, 1872.

<!-- page 593 -->
Upon cancellation of the sale of Island No. 3 to Mr. Powell, a claim for certain disbursements made by him in
connection with the purchase was presented to the Department through his solicitors, Messrs. Nickle, Farrell & Day, of
Kingston. A copy of this claim is attached hereto, and with reference particularly to the item of $50, the explanation
given is that the expenditure was incurred in the purchase of dynamite for the purpose of blasting a sheltered harbour
for a motor-boat.

With reference to the third and last paragraph of your letter, you are correct in assuming that the certification of the
Justice Department on the 24th of January, 1923, was intended to show that in the opinion of that Department, Mr.
Powell had a legal claim against this department for the sum of $81.55, as itemized in the statement hereto appended.

Your obedient servant,
DUNCAN C. SCOTT, Deputy Supt. General.

The Assistant Auditor General, Ottawa.

AUDIT OFFICE, OTTAWA, October 30th, 1923.

SIR, - I beg to acknowledge receipt of your letter of the 12th inst. (File 87, 235/1A) in reply to mine of the 9th inst.,
with respect to the payment of $81.55 to Carroll Haffell Powell to reimburse him for certain expenditures incurred by
him in connection with the sale to him of Little Horse Shoe Island, which sale was subsequently cancelled.

One of the items covered by this payment is a claim of $50 for dynamite purchased by him for the purpose of blasting
a sheltered harbour for a motor boat. I think that this item should be supported by a receipted account or by other
documentary evidence that this amount has been actually expended by Mr. Powell. It does not appear from the
correspondence that the dynamite purchased was actually used at Little Horse Shoe Island. If it were not so used I do
not think that Mr. Powell should be allowed to retain the dynamite in addition to being reimbursed for its purchase.

I am, sir, your obedient servant,
WM. KEARNS, Asst. A.G.

The Deputy Superintendent General of Indian Affairs, Ottawa.

Payment towards Construction of Provincial Highways

AUDIT OFFICE, OTTAWA, June, 23, 1923.

SIR, - Nova Scotia Cheque No. 615, drawn on December 12, 1922, is for the payment of $3,000 to the Town of Truro
as partial cost of reconstructing 3,325 feet of Halifax-Truro highway through Millbrook Indian Reserve.

From a letter from the Town Clerk of Truro, which is attached to the voucher, I infer that this reserve is included in
the Town of Truro, and that the total cost of that part of the road which passes through the reserve was $3,495.

1 - 16 1/2 I
